modelAnswer: There are three types of RNA. Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the genetic message copied from DNA out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm, where it is used for protein synthesis. Transfer RNA (tRNA) transfers specific amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis, matching each amino acid to the correct codon on the mRNA. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a structural component of the ribosome; it combines with ribosomal proteins to build the ribosome subunits, which act as the cell's protein-making factories. All three types work together during translation to convert genetic information into proteins.

keyPoints: DNA is double-stranded, ladder-like, coiled into a helix; strands are antiparallel.
Sugar-phosphate backbone forms the uprights; nitrogenous bases form the rungs.
Chargaff-style rule: adenine = thymine, cytosine = guanine in amount.
Specific complementary base pairing: A-T, C-G, via hydrogen bonds (2 between A-T, 3 between C-G).
Uniform diameter of about 2 nm.
modelAnswer: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA. Its main points are: (1) DNA is double-stranded, like a ladder, with both strands coiled around each other in a helix. (2) The two strands run antiparallel, meaning they are oriented in opposite directions to each other. (3) The backbone (the uprights of the ladder) of each strand is made of alternating sugar and phosphate groups, while the nitrogenous bases form the rungs of the ladder. (4) The amount of adenine always equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of cytosine always equals the amount of guanine. (5) Base pairing between the two strands is highly specific: adenine on one strand always pairs with thymine on the other, and cytosine always pairs with guanine; because of this rule, the base sequence of one strand is complementary to the sequence of the other. (6) The two strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds: two hydrogen bonds form between adenine and thymine, and three form between cytosine and guanine. (7) The double helix has a uniform diameter of about 2 nanometres throughout its length.
stem: Explain double helix structure of DNA proposed by Watson and Crick.

modelAnswer: DNA and RNA differ in at least six features. Strandedness: DNA is double-stranded (two strands coiled as a helix); RNA is single-stranded. Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose sugar; RNA contains ribose sugar. Bases: DNA uses thymine as one of its four bases; RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. Base overhangs: in RNA the nitrogen bases are overhung because they are not bonded to a complementary strand, unlike in DNA where every base is paired. Location/role: DNA is found in the nucleus (in chromosomes) and stores and passes on genetic information; RNA is synthesised in the nucleus but moves to the cytoplasm, acting as an intermediate that carries out protein synthesis. Formation: RNA is synthesised from a DNA template by copying (transcribing) the sequence of one DNA strand.

topicTitle: 6.11 Flow of Genetic Information from DNA to RNA and Then to Proteins
keyPoints: DNA writes, RNA delivers, ribosome builds
Support each claim with the quoted textbook line
modelAnswer: A gene directs protein synthesis in two steps. In transcription the gene's DNA unwinds and its message is copied into messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus. In translation ribosomes read that message three bases at a time and assemble the matching amino acids into the protein. The gene thus fixes both the identity and the order of amino acids in every protein the cell makes.

topicTitle: 6.11 Flow of Genetic Information from DNA to RNA and Then to Proteins
keyPoints: Dogma direction: DNA, RNA, protein
Support each claim with the quoted textbook line
modelAnswer: The central dogma states the one-way flow of biological information: DNA makes RNA makes protein. A gene's base sequence is transcribed into messenger RNA inside the nucleus; the mRNA moves to ribosomes where transfer RNAs read each codon and line up the right amino acids. The gene's role is decisive here, since its sequence alone dictates which amino acids join and in what order, ending as a working protein.
